power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A priori power analysis (two-tailed Pearson product-moment correlation, power = 0.80, α = 0.05, ρ = 0.30) was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007). The analysis indicated that a minimum sample size of 84 participants was required. This study recruited a total of 247 university students online. Nineteen participants were excluded from the final sample for failing to follow the task instructions. The final sample therefore consisted of 228 participants (158 females), with a mean age of 19.89 years (SD = 0.55). All participants provided online informed consent prior to the survey and received course credits for their participation.
table.header: 2.1.1 Participants

table.text: A priori power analysis (Pearson's chi-square test for a 2 × 2 contingency table, power = 0.80, α = 0.05, Cohen's w = 0.30, df = 1) was conducted using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2007). The analysis indicated that a minimum total sample size of 88 participants was required. This study recruited a total of 90 native Mandarin Chinese speakers. Seven participants were excluded from the final sample for failing to follow the task instructions. The final sample consisted of 83 participants (M = 19.88, SD = 0.43; 69 females), randomly assigned to either the creative activity group (n = 40) or the control group (n = 43). All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and provided written informed consent prior to the experiment. Participants received participation gifts, course credit, and ¥3 for their participation.

The final sample therefore consisted of 94 participants (ages: M = 19.86, SD = 1.22; 76 females), with 49 assigned to the creative activity group and 45 to the control group. All participants had normal or corrected-tonormal vision and received ¥10 for their participation.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Creative engagement may shape not only the ideas people generate but also their willingness to take calculated risks in subsequent decisions, yet this possibility remains underexplored.
Across three studies, we examined this relationship and whether general self-efficacy or affective state accounts for the relationship.
Study 1 (N = 228) used a cross-sectional survey and found that everyday creative ideation behavior was positively associated with overall and domain-specific risk-taking propensity.
General self-efficacy did not mediate this association.
Study 2 (N = 83) experimentally compared calculated risk taking after creative drawing versus standard coloring using a binary lottery choice.
Creative drawing increased affective dominance but did not significantly influence calculated risk taking.
Study 3 (N = 94) compared calculated risk taking after creative writing versus standard typing using a six-level investmentchoice task.
Creative writing increased both calculated risk taking and affective dominance, but the change in dominance did not mediate the effect on calculated risk taking.
These findings suggest that creative engagement can influence subsequent calculated risk taking, although the effect may depend on the creative task and the sensitivity of the risk measure.
Neither general self-efficacy nor affective dominance explained this relationship, highlighting the need to investigate alternative psychological mechanisms.
When developing a novel idea, composing a novel story, or drawing a novel image, the creators must move beyond safe and conventional responses and pursue untested possibilities that may fail.

Creative activity, the process of generating ideas or products that are both novel and useful or appropriate (Runco & Jaeger, 2012), therefore involves an element of risk taking, broadly defined as engaging in behaviors or making choices under uncertainty that may produce beneficial or adverse consequences (Duell & Steinberg, 2020; Trimpop, 1994).
text.formatted: Creative activity, the process of generating ideas or products that are both novel and useful or appropriate <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Runco & Jaeger, 2012)</ref>, therefore involves an element of risk taking, broadly defined as engaging in behaviors or making choices under uncertainty that may produce beneficial or adverse consequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Duell & Steinberg, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Trimpop, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this overlap, creativity and risk taking have long been regarded as closely related (Bonetto et al., 2020; Crepaldi et al., 2024; Graciano et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Consistent with this overlap, creativity and risk taking have long been regarded as closely related <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bonetto et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Crepaldi et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Graciano et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Yet existing research has largely examined this relationship through stable individual differences in creative personality, creative ability, and risk-taking propensity.

It therefore remains unclear whether creative engagement itself influences subsequent risk takin, particularly calculated risk taking involving deliberate consideration of potential outcomes (Zhang & Smith, 2025).
text.formatted: It therefore remains unclear whether creative engagement itself influences subsequent risk takin, particularly calculated risk taking involving deliberate consideration of potential outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Zhang & Smith, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If it does, creative engagement may influence later innovation and decisions beyond the creative task, suggesting that it is not merely a source of creative output but also an experience that shapes subsequent decision makings.
The present research primarily addresses this question by examining whether brief creative engagement can influence subsequent calculated risk taking.
Research has examined the relationship between creativity and risk taking in both directions.
One line of research has examined risk taking as an antecedent or facilitating condition for creativity (Beghetto et al., 2021; Dewett, 2006; Graciano et al., 2023; Harada, 2020; Shen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: One line of research has examined risk taking as an antecedent or facilitating condition for creativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beghetto et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Dewett, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Graciano et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Harada, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Shen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Within entrepreneurial and educational contexts, risk taking has been conceptualized as a facilitating condition that helps translate creativity into innovation (Graciano et al., 2023). Park et al. (2024) found that employees generated more ideas on days when their felt responsibility for change and willingness to take risks were both high, and daily idea generation statistically mediated the association between this motivational congruence and creative performance. Beghetto et al. (2021) further reported that intellectual risk taking strengthened the association between creative confidence and creative behavior.

(2021)</ref> further reported that intellectual risk taking strengthened the association between creative confidence and creative behavior.

text.text: In addition, research also probed the relationships between risk taking, divergent thinking and convergent thinking performance.

While Shen et al. (2018) found that lower risk taking was only associated with better convergent thinking performance, Harada (2020) found that risk taking was only associated with better divergent thinking performance.

(2018)</ref> found that lower risk taking was only associated with better convergent thinking performance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Harada (2020)</ref> found that risk taking was only associated with better divergent thinking performance.

text.text: A recent finding indicated that willingness to take creative risks was positively related to originality but negatively related to usefulness, with creative metacognition strengthening the former association and attenuating the latter (Woo & Lee, 2024).
text.formatted: A recent finding indicated that willingness to take creative risks was positively related to originality but negatively related to usefulness, with creative metacognition strengthening the former association and attenuating the latter <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Woo & Lee, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, these findings generally suggest that a willingness to take risks can facilitate creativity, although its benefits may vary across creative outcomes.

Another line of research has considered the reverse direction, investigating whether creativity is associated with risk taking (Bonetto et al., 2020; Crepaldi et al., 2024; Tyagi et al., 2017). Charyton et al. (2013) found that creative attributes (unconventional, insightful, confident, inventive, reflective, and broad interests) were associated with greater willingness to express unconventional ideas despite possible criticism or reputational costs. Tyagi et al. (2017) found that several measures of creativity were most consistently related to social risk taking, whereas their associations with financial, ethical, health, and recreational risks were weaker or inconsistent. Bonetto et al. (2020) further observed such positive associations between measures of creativity and social risk taking.

text.text: A recent review also suggest an overall positive relationship between creativity and risk taking, suggesting people with lower creativity tend to avoid risky situations and decisions, while highly-creative individuals tend not to flinch from challenging situations (Crepaldi et al., 2024).

text.text: These findings indicate that creativity-related traits and abilities are also closely associated with individuals' willingness to take risks.

Taken together, existing research has mostly either treated risk taking as an antecedent of creativity or examined cross-sectional associations between risk taking and relatively stable creative traits and abilities.
However, these associations may partly reflect shared personality dispositions, particularly openness to experience.

Research has shown that openness to experience is not only positively associated with divergent thinking (Grajzel et al., 2023), predicts everyday creative activity (Jauk et al., 2014), and is the Big Five trait most strongly associated with risk propensity (Highhouse et al., 2022).

text.text: These shared dispositional correlates limit the interpretation of existing findings.

In addition, recent research distinguishes calculated from spontaneous risk taking: the former involves deliberate and planned risk taking after careful consideration of outcomes, whereas the latter is impulsive, emotion-driven, and thrill seeking, with little deliberation (Zhang & Smith, 2025).
text.formatted: In addition, recent research distinguishes calculated from spontaneous risk taking: the former involves deliberate and planned risk taking after careful consideration of outcomes, whereas the latter is impulsive, emotion-driven, and thrill seeking, with little deliberation <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Zhang & Smith, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Previous creativity research has rarely differentiated these two styles, leaving their respective relationships with creativity unclear.
Calculated risk taking is particularly relevant because creative work often requires intentionally pursuing uncertain but potentially valuable ideas after weighing their possible costs and benefits.

Therefore, to enrich understanding of the relationship between creativity and risk taking, experimental research is needed to determine whether creative engagement itself influences subsequent calculated risk taking.
Although direct evidence remains limited, the psychological consequences of creative engagement provide a basis for expecting such an effect on subsequent calculated risk taking.
Evidence has already shown that creative engagement changes how people feel and experience themselves during and after the creative process.
Creative ideation increased participants' feeling of autonomy, although it also heightened concern about how their ideas would be evaluated (Kim et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Creative ideation increased participants' feeling of autonomy, although it also heightened concern about how their ideas would be evaluated <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kim et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: A multigroup randomized study similarly found that creative tasks increased positive emotion partly through enhancing autonomous self-expression (Bujacz et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A multigroup randomized study similarly found that creative tasks increased positive emotion partly through enhancing autonomous self-expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bujacz et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Even brief creative activities have been associated with improved mood.

For instance, creating a mandala reduced negative affect relative to a control activity (Babouchkina & Robbins, 2015), and a single session of open-studio art making was followed by higher positive affect and lower negative affect (Kaimal & Ray, 2017).

text.text: Besides, positive and negative affect also change over the course of a creative task rather than only at its end (Montag-Smit & Keith, 2023).
text.formatted: Besides, positive and negative affect also change over the course of a creative task rather than only at its end <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Montag-Smit & Keith, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, daily creative activity is also associated with changes in affective state.
Results showed that daily creativity also predicts higher activated positive affect and flourishing on the following day (Conner et al., 2018; Conner & Silvia, 2015; Smith et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Results showed that daily creativity also predicts higher activated positive affect and flourishing on the following day <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Conner et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Conner & Silvia, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Smith et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: More recent experience-sampling evidence showed that everyday creative engagement was accompanied by greater autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which in turn were associated with higher positive affect (Putney et al., 2024), and people were more likely to engage in everyday creative activity on days when they felt happy and energetic (Silvia et al., 2014).

text.text: Population research found that people who participated more frequently in creative and cultural activities reported higher well-being. (Cuypers et al., 2012; Fancourt & Finn, 2019; Finn et al., 2025).

text.text: These findings indicate that both brief and sustained creative engagement can shape individuals' affective experiences.

Beyond its effects on affective experience, creative engagement may also influence subsequent decision making. Krause et al. (2024) found brief creative ideation increased subsequent reward seeking and indulgent choices, partly through activation of the behavioral approach system. Xu et al. (2021) found that engaging in a creative activity enhanced individuals' feeling of autonomy, thus inducing a positive affective state, which in turn led to higher donation behaviors. Charness and Grieco (2022) recently found that participants who completed creative rather than routine tasks exhibited greater ambiguity tolerance during a monetary lottery.

text.formatted: Creative engagement even induced a preference for horror entertainment through higher self-efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Yang & Liu, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These experiments indicate that creative engagement can carry over to subsequent decisions through affective and cognitive-motivational processes.
Overall, research on the affective and decision-related consequences of creative engagement provides converging grounds for expecting it to influence subsequent calculated risk-taking behavior.
Yet, much less is known about whether creative engagement influences subsequent calculated risk-taking behavior and, if so, through what candidate psychological pathways.

General self-efficacy, the broad belief that one can manage challenges and reach a goal (Bandura, 1977; Luszczynska et al., 2005; Schwarzer & Jerusalem, 1995), may serve as a plausible pathway linking creative engagement to calculated risk taking.

text.text: Self-efficacy has also been shown to mediate the effect of creative engagement on subsequent preference for horror entertainment, although the outcome did not involve a conventional risktaking decision (Yang & Liu, 2024).

text.text: These studies suggest that creative engagement may strengthen general self-efficacy, which could increase willingness to pursue uncertain or challenging options.
However, whether general self-efficacy explains the effect of creative engagement on calculated risk-taking decisions remains unknown.
Changes in affective state may provide another pathway through which creative engagement influences subsequent calculated risk taking.
Within the Pleasure-Arousal-Dominance Framework, affective state is characterized along three dimensions: pleasure, arousal, and dominance (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974; Russell & Mehrabian, 1977).

text.text: Pleasure reflects hedonic valence, arousal reflects the level of activation, and dominance reflects the subjective experience of being in control rather than controlled in a given situation (Bakker et al., 2014; Mehrabian, 1996).

text.text: Previous research suggests that engaging in creative activities can enhance positive affect and strengthen individuals' sense of autonomy (Kim et al., 2023; Montag-Smit & Keith, 2023; Putney et al., 2024).

text.text: Because open-ended creative tasks permit self-directed decisions about how ideas are developed, the autonomy afforded by creative engagement may also temporarily heighten felt control or affective dominance.
Moreover, research has also shown that affective responses can influence subsequent decision making.

text.text: The Appraisal-Tendency Framework further suggests that affective states shape subsequent judgments not only through their pleasure but also through the situational appraisals they carry, including certainty, responsibility, and control (Han et al., 2007; Lerner & Keltner, 2001; Lerner et al., 2015).

text.text: Together, these accounts suggest that affective states influence risk taking not only through valence but also through appraisals of certainty and control, suggesting affective state, especially affective dominance, as a theoretically candidate pathway linking creative engagement to subsequent calculated risk taking.
This study also aimed to explore whether changes in affective states mediated the effect of creative engagement on calculated risk-taking decisions.
The present research examined whether creative engagement can influence subsequent risk-taking behavior through three studies.
We further investigated general self-efficacy and affective state as two potential psychological pathways underlying this relationship.

As a preliminary study, Study 1 used a cross-sectional survey to examine whether everyday creative engagement was positively associated with general risktaking propensity and the potential mediating role of general self-efficacy.

Studies 2 and 3 narrowed the investigation to calculated risk taking by experimentally testing whether brief creative engagement influenced subsequent financial risk decisions, in which potential gains and losses were explicitly presented.
They also examined whether changes in affective state accounted for this effect.
In Study 2, participants completed either a creative drawing task or a standard coloring task before making a binary lottery choice with real monetary consequences.
Study 3 extended the experimental investigation by comparing creative writing with standard typing and using an investment-choice task comprising six ordered levels of risk and expected return.

Together, these studies examined the relationship between creative engagement and calculated risk taking, as well as the potential underlying psychological pathways, across different research designs, creative modalities, and measures of risk taking.
The specific hypotheses are presented in the corresponding study sections.
The study protocols were approved by the Ethics Committee of XXX University (masked for peer review; ID: 2025060) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

We proposed the following hypotheses: (H1) creative engagement would be positively associated with risk-taking propensity; and (H2) general self-efficacy would statistically mediate this association.

Given that monetary paradigms allow probabilities and potential outcomes to be explicitly specified and provide a direct behavioral measure of calculated risk taking, a monetary choice task was used in this study.
Participants were randomly assigned to complete either a creative drawing task or a standard coloring control task before making a binary lottery choice with real monetary consequences.

Affective states were measured before and after the activity to examine whether the creative activity altered participants' affective state and whether change in affective state mediated the effect of creative activity on calculated risk taking.

Risk-taking decision task.
Calculated risk-taking behavior was assessed using a lottery task with real monetary consequences.
Participants received a ¥3 endowment and chose between keeping it as a guaranteed payment or exchanging it for a 10% chance of receiving ¥10 and a 90% chance of receiving nothing.
Before making their choice, participants estimated the proportion of the wheel occupied by a red area and their subjective probability of winning, both on a scale from 0‰ to 1000‰.
Lottery entry was coded as 1 and non-entry as 0.
Participants who entered the lottery proceeded to a computerized roulette wheel, with outcomes generated independently for each participant at a fixed 10% winning probability.
Course credit and the participation gift were unaffected by lottery outcomes.
Affective states.
Affective states were assessed using the Self-Assessment Manikin (Bradley & Lang, 1994), a nonverbal pictorial self-report measure of pleasure, arousal, and dominance.

text.text: Each dimension was rated on a 9-point scale.
Pleasure ranged from very unpleasant (1) to very pleasant (9), arousal from very calm (1) to very excited (9), and dominance from feeling controlled (1) to feeling in control (9).
Subjective creative experience was assessed with a single item: "While coloring the elephants, I tried to be as creative as possible."
Responses were made on a 7-point scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater perceived creativity during the task.
General self-efficacy was also assessed using the same 10item General Self-Efficacy Scale used in Study 1.
Internal consistency was .86 in the present sample.
This study employed a one-factor, two-level between-subjects design, with participants randomly assigned to either a creative activity group or a control group.

Following the drawing paradigm of Xu et al. (2021), participants in the creative activity group completed a 6-min creative drawing task, whereas those in the control group completed a 6-min standard coloring task.

text.text: The experiment was conducted individually in a quiet laboratory.
Upon arrival, participants were seated at a table and provided written informed consent.
They first completed the demographic measures and the pretest of affective states.

Next, participants in the creative activity group used multicolored crayons to color and decorate two elephant outlines, whereas those in the control group used only a gray crayon to completely fill in both outlines.
Paper size, outline dimensions and placement, and the experimental setting were held constant across participants.
Participants in the creative activity group received the following instructions: You now have a box of crayons in different colors and two blank elephant pictures.
You may use any number and any color of crayons to color and decorate the elephants.
Be as creative as possible and create two unique elephants.
Do not worry about whether your drawings are conventional or realistic.
Participants in the control group received the following instructions: You now have a gray crayon and two blank elephant pictures.
Please use the gray crayon to color the elephants and completely fill in both pictures.
During the task, the experimenter provided no feedback regarding the aesthetic quality, completeness, or creativity of the drawings.
After the drawing task, participants rated their subjective creative experience and posttest of affective states, followed by measures of general self-efficacy.
Finally, participants completed the risk-taking decision task, which comprised a visual areaestimation task, a subjective winning-probability judgment, and a lottery choice.

The creative activity increased affective dominance, but change in dominance did not predict calculated risk taking, and the mediating effect was not significant.
Therefore, Hypothesis 4 was partially supported, but Hypothesis 5 was not supported.

text.text: Participants received a ¥10 cash endowment and selected one of six investment options.
They were informed that potential gains or losses resulting from their choice would affect the amount they ultimately received.

They could retain the full endowment without investing or select investment A, B, C, D, or E. These investments offered average returns of 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, and 25%, with possible returns ranging from -15% to 25%, -30% to 50%, -45% to 75%, -60% to 100%, and -75% to 125%, respectively.
Choices were coded from 0 (no investment) to 5 (investment E), with higher scores indicating a selection of riskier investment options.
Although participants believed that their choices had real monetary consequences, all ultimately retained the ¥10 endowment after the experiment, regardless of their choice.
The participants were fully debriefed after the experiment.

Keyword presentation, text-box dimensions and position, and all other experimental settings were held constant across groups.
In both groups, the same set of keywords (i.e.
Task A: moon, tree shadows, and song; Task B: campus, basketball, pencil case) was displayed at the top of the computer screen.

Participants in the creative activity group wrote a short story incorporating all the keywords and were instructed to imagine vivid scenes, be as creative as possible, and not be constrained by realism.
Participants in the control group transcribed a provided paragraph containing the same keywords into the text box without revising, elaborating, or adding original content.
After the tasks, participants rated their subjective creative experience and affective states, then completed the general selfefficacy scale.
They subsequently received ¥10 in cash and signed a receipt acknowledging payment before choosing whether to retain the money or select one of five investment options (A-E).

Data were analyzed using SPSS 26.0 and R 4.6.0.
Independent-samples t tests compared the two groups on baseline risk-taking propensity and subjective creative experience, with the latter serving as a manipulation check.
To test Hypothesis III, the calculated risk taking was firstly submitted to an independent-samples t test with GROUP as the between-subject factor.
Next, an ordinal logistic regression model with a cumulative logit link was fitted to the calculated risk taking, with GROUP as the predictor, controlling for gender and general self-efficacy.
The proportional odds assumption was assessed using a likelihood-ratio test of parallel lines.

To test Hypothesis IV, separate 2 (TIME: pretest vs. posttest) × 2 (GROUP: creative activity vs. control) mixed-design ANOVAs were conducted to assess changes in affective pleasure, arousal, and dominance, followed by simple-effects analyses where appropriate.

To test Hypothesis V, a mediation analysis was conducted to examine whether the change in affective dominance mediated the effect of GROUP on the calculated risk taking, adjusting for gender and general self-efficacy.

Study 3 found that the creative writing task induced a stronger subjective creative experience, and led participants to select investment options with higher risk (for higher returns) than the standard typing task.
Hypothesis 3 was supported in Study 3.
This group difference remained significant in the ordinal logistic regression after adjusting for gender and general self-efficacy.

Moreover, creative performance was not significantly associated with calculated risk taking, suggesting that the observed increase in calculated risk taking was associated with creative engagement rather than the quality of participants' creative output.

Affective dominance also increased selectively in the creative activity group, but it did not predict calculated risk taking or mediate the association between creative activity and calculated risk taking.
Therefore, Hypothesis 4 was partially supported, but Hypothesis 5 was not supported.

The present research examined whether creative engagement is associated with and can influence subsequent calculated risk taking, as well as whether general selfefficacy and affective state account for this relationship.

Study 1 showed that everyday creative engagement was positively associated with overall risk-taking propensity and with domain-specific forms of risk taking, even after controlling for gender and general self-efficacy.
General self-efficacy, however, did not mediate this association.
Hypothesis 1 was supported, but Hypothesis 2 was not supported.
Study 2 showed that a brief creative drawing activity increased affective dominance but did not significantly affect calculated risk taking in a binary monetary lottery.
Study 3 extended the experimental investigation using a verbal creative writing task and a more differentiated investment-choice measure.
Participants who completed the creative writing task selected higher-risk, higher-return investment options than those who completed the standard typing task.
Creative writing also increased affective dominance, but this change did not mediate the effect on calculated risk taking.
Collectively, Hypothesis 3 and 4 was partially supported, but Hypothesis 5 was not supported.
Results showed that everyday creative engagement was positively associated with overall risk-taking propensity and a brief creative writing activity could increase subsequent calculated risk taking.
The results extend previous research by examining creative engagement as a possible antecedent of subsequent risk taking (Bonetto et al., 2020; Crepaldi et al., 2024).

text.text: The present research extends these studies by examining whether visual and verbal creative activities affect subsequent calculated risk taking using both a binary lottery choice and a graded investment choice.

The results provide initial evidence that, under some task conditions, even risk taking involving explicit evaluation of potential outcomes can be shaped by prior creative engagement, thereby refining our understanding of the relationship between creative engagement and risk taking.

Study 1 also showed that everyday creative engagement was positively associated with risk-taking propensity across six specific domains: ethical, investment, gambling, health/safety, recreational, and social risk taking.

This broader pattern extends the findings of Tyagi et al. (2017), who observed the most consistent associations between creativity and social risk taking, with weaker or less consistent associations in the financial, ethical, health/safety, and recreational domains.

text.text: This finding raises the possibility that creative engagement may influence multiple forms of risk taking beyond calculated financial decisions.
Future experimental research should test this possibility across different risk domains.
Study 3 further showed that creative performance was not significantly correlated with calculated risk taking.
Although this null correlation should be interpreted cautiously, it may imply that engaging in the creative activity matters more than the quality of the creative outcomes.

The mediation results in Study 1 did not support general self-efficacy as an explanation for the relationship between creative engagement and risk-taking propensity.
Creative ideation behavior was positively associated with general selfefficacy, but general self-efficacy did not predict overall risk-taking propensity after the other variables were considered.

This pattern suggests that self-efficacy may be more likely to increase when creative engagement provides a clear experience of competence.

Future research could examine more specific processes, such as reward sensitivity and behavioral activation (Krause et al., 2024), tolerance of ambiguity (Charness & Grieco, 2022), and perceived control over decision outcomes (Damen, 2019; Langer, 1975; Moore, 2016).

text.text: Theoretically, the central contribution of the present research is to recast creative engagement from an outcome to be explained into an experience that may shape subsequent decision making.
Previous research has repeatedly reported positive correlation between risk taking and creativity, while their associations may partly reflect shared characteristics such as openness to experience.
The present research provides evidence that this relationship is not limited to stable individual differences.
Under some task conditions, engaging in a creative activity can influence subsequent calculated risk taking.

The findings therefore extend creativity research by identifying a potential behavioral spillover from creative engagement to subsequent choices involving explicit calculated risk-return trade-offs, complementing previously documented effects on ambiguity tolerance, indulgent choices, charitable giving, and entertainment preferences (Charness & Grieco, 2022; Krause et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2021; Yang & Liu, 2024).

text.text: Practically, in education, open-ended creative activities may help students become more comfortable considering uncertain alternatives, although their long-term effects on calculated risk taking require longitudinal evidence.
In scientific, entrepreneurial, organizational, and governmental settings, creative engagement may similarly encourage experimentation when excessive caution impedes innovation.
Conversely, sustained involvement in highly routine activities might contribute to more conservative decision patterns, but this possibility remains to be tested.
Individuals and organizations should therefore recognize creative engagement as a possible influence on subsequent choices and retain explicit evaluation criteria when the stakes are high.
Several questions remain for future research.

First, although Study 1 indicated that everyday creative engagement was associated with risk-taking propensity across multiple domains, the experiments focused exclusively on calculated monetary risk taking.
Experimental research is therefore needed to determine whether the effect extends to other types of calculated risk taking.
Second, although random assignment in Studies 2 and 3 should have reduced systematic between-condition differences in openness to experience, this trait was not measured.
Future research should assess openness to verify baseline equivalence and examine whether it moderates the effect of creative engagement.
Third, the experimental studies focused on calculated risk taking through financial decisions involving explicit potential outcomes.
Whether creative engagement also influences spontaneous risk taking remains to be examined (Zhang & Smith, 2025).
text.formatted: Whether creative engagement also influences spontaneous risk taking remains to be examined <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Zhang & Smith, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, the experiments also captured only the immediate consequences of brief creative engagement, leaving open whether sustained creative engagement shapes consequential real-world behavior over time.
Fifth, the psychological mechanism that underlies the creative engagement effect also remains unresolved.

Research with more sensitive process measures and multimodal methods, including psychophysiological measures, electroencephalography, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (Lu & Hao, 2026; Strouthos et al., 2025), may help clarify the neuro-cognitive processes linking creative engagement to subsequent calculated risk taking.
